title: Lesson 4: Discriminant
central_question: Before you finish solving, how can you tell from the equation alone whether the curve will hit the x-axis twice, once, or not at all — and which solve strategy is worth using?
intended_understanding: The discriminant D = b^2 − 4ac predicts the number of real roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (positive → two, zero → one, negative → none), and those real roots match the graph’s x-intercepts. Students evaluate D, connect it to intercepts, and complete the Module 4 share of strategy comparison (graphing · factoring · quadratic formula). The formula itself is review-only here (apply to illustrate cases); completing the square is not retaught; full applications wait for Lesson 5.
prerequisite_assumptions: Students can apply the quadratic formula using technology to find real roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (Module 4 Lesson 3; A1.6 apply). Formula development is not retaught; apply-for-cases is REVIEW only.

Students can determine real roots by graphing and by factoring (Module 3 Lessons 2–3; A1.8 M3 share). This lesson completes the Module 4 strategy comparison by adding the formula and the discriminant as decision tools; it does not reteach graphing or factoring.
Students already have intercept / feature language from Module 3 and Lessons 1–2 (A1.5, A2.10). Completing the square and transformations are assumed known and are not retaught.
Students can read a, b, and c from a standard-zero equation, rearranging when needed (Module 4 Lesson 3). Discriminant evaluation uses that same triple.
processes_to_teach: discriminant-evaluate: Evaluate D = b^2 − 4ac for a quadratic already written as ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
discriminant-to-number-of-real-roots: Connect the sign of D to the number of real roots (positive → two, zero → one, negative → none).

roots-to-x-intercepts-link: Relate the real roots of the equation to the x-intercepts of the corresponding graph, using the seed language that there are no real roots and no x-intercepts if b^2 − 4ac < 0.
predict-from-D-then-verify-graph (light): Predict the number of x-intercepts from D, then verify lightly on a graph — not a full sketch-from-standard lesson.

strategy-compare-graph-factor-formula: Complete the Module 4 share of A1.8 — determine real roots of a variety of quadratic equations and describe advantages and disadvantages of graphing, factoring, and using the quadratic formula.
apply-formula-review-for-cases (REVIEW only): Apply the quadratic formula (with technology as in Lesson 3) only to illustrate discriminant cases. Not new teach of the formula or its development.

purpose_map.purpose: Put students in a situation where they need to know, from the equation alone, whether the curve hits the x-axis twice, once, or not at all — before they finish solving. Tiny how-many-solutions context only; not Lesson 5 modelling. Completing the square is not practiced.
Re-apply the Lesson 3 quadratic formula (REVIEW only) on one standard-zero equation so a, b, and c are live before D is named. Do not reteach formula development. (Apply: formula-review)

Fully demonstrate evaluating D = b^2 − 4ac and connecting its sign to the number of real roots on the same example. Cognitive targets Apply then Understand. (discriminant-evaluate; discriminant-to-number-of-real-roots)

Relate those real roots to the x-intercepts of the corresponding graph. Use the seed language: there are no real roots and no x-intercepts if b^2 − 4ac < 0. Cognitive target Understand. (roots-to-x-intercepts-link)
Predict the number of x-intercepts from D, then verify lightly on a graph. Light only — not A2.11 sketch-from-standard. Cognitive target Apply. (predict-from-D-then-verify-graph)

Repeat D → number of real roots → intercept link on a second and third case that vary the sign of D, so the first example is not a template to copy. Stay inside real-root language; no complex arithmetic. (Apply / Understand)

Complete the Module 4 share of A1.8: on a short variety of equations, determine real roots and describe advantages and disadvantages of graphing, factoring, and using the quadratic formula — with D as a decision cue. Cognitive target Evaluate. (strategy-compare-graph-factor-formula)

Return to the hook: evaluate D from the equation, name how many times the curve hits the x-axis, choose a solve strategy with a reason, and retrieve that D < 0 means no real roots and no x-intercepts.

hook_constraint: Tiny how-many-solutions context is allowed; this is not full A3 modelling (A3.2 / A3.3). Do not practice completing the square. Prefer a lean Mobbin + Wonder visual if a hook visual is used. No complex arithmetic beyond the seed language (no real roots and no x-intercepts if b^2 − 4ac < 0). Consolidation must return to that same situation. No required login, Gizmos, or Desmos API. No Nelson discriminant stems.
instructional_sequence_intent: Need how-many-hits from the equation alone (hook) → L3 formula apply REVIEW → worked D + number of real roots → roots-to-x-intercepts link (seed D<0 language) → predict from D then verify on a graph (light) → varied D cases → A1.8 complete compare (graphing · factoring · formula) → consolidation returns to hook with Key Idea / Need to Know.

representations.note: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 as the writing from which a, b, c and D are read.
D = b^2 − 4ac as the predictor of the number of real roots.
Real roots as x-intercepts; used to verify a D prediction and to contrast graphing as a strategy.
Name the number of real roots, the intercept link (including D < 0), and advantages/disadvantages of graphing, factoring, and the formula.
Technology to apply the formula for review cases and/or to check a graph against a D prediction.
Formula apply is REVIEW only to illustrate cases; not a production target and not a development reteach.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students flip the sign of D (or of b^2 − 4ac) and then name the wrong number of real roots.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students treat D as if it were the quadratic formula, or they substitute D into x = (−b ± √D) / (2a) without first deciding whether real roots exist.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students think D < 0 means there is no parabola, rather than no real roots and no x-intercepts.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students default to the formula on every equation, skipping the A1.8 comparison of graphing, factoring, and the formula.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students (or a later writer) push past the seed language into complex-number arithmetic when D < 0, instead of stopping at no real roots and no x-intercepts.
